November 2035. Dr Vogt moved into the first floor of number 33, right above the café, a month ago. He knocks on Ludwig's door with a letter in his hand.
Good evening, Mr Brandt. Sorry to disturb you. I'm Konrad Vogt, from number thirty-three, first floor, right above the café. I'm afraid I have to complain about something.

About the bell. The brass bell in the café. Anyone who comes in is allowed to ring it. It even says so on a sign. I work nights at the hospital and sleep during the day. And every day it rings beneath me forty, fifty times.
I understand. I'm sorry. I fully understand your annoyance. I worked shifts for years myself.
I don't want to spoil anyone's fun. But I've read the house rules, and they say it's quiet time between one and three. Nobody sticks to that.
You're right. Still, I have to tell you that this bell is very important to a lot of people here. It belonged to my old tram.
I didn't know that. Still, I need my sleep. Would it be possible to take the bell down, at least during the day?

I wouldn't want to take it down. But I'll suggest something else. Would you be willing to sit down tomorrow with my granddaughter? The café is hers. I'm sure we'll find a solution everyone can live with.
All right. We can agree on that. At eleven? After that I have to sleep.
At eleven. And, Doctor: thank you for coming to me first and not going straight to the landlord.

The next morning at eleven, Dr Konrad Vogt was sitting in the café «Bei Ingrid» at the window table, right at the back, as far as possible from the brass bell, drinking a mint tea, because, as he explained, coffee after a night shift is the last thing he needs. He was a tall, thin man of about forty-five, with greying temples and very tired eyes, and he was still wearing the jacket he had come from the hospital in, with a small badge on the lapel that he had forgotten to take off. It said: “Dr. K. Vogt, Anästhesie” (anaesthesia). Lena sat down opposite him, with a little notebook and a feeling in her stomach she hadn't had since her master baker's exam.

Ludwig had told her everything the evening before. He had also told her what he thought of the new neighbour: “A serious man. But not an unfriendly one. He knocked on the door first, before writing a letter. That's rare these days.” Lena had lain awake half the night thinking about what she would say. The bell wasn't just any bell. It had hung by the till since the day of the reopening, and every child on Kastanienallee knew that you were allowed to ring it when you came in, once if something good had happened to you and twice if you'd been through something sad. That had been Hotte's rule, and it had spread along the street faster than any rumour.

During the night, when he couldn't sleep, Andrei had given her a piece of advice that, as he said, he knew from his negotiations with the BVG, when he was developing his app for step-free stops. “Don't start with your arguments,” he had said. “Start with his. First tell him where he's right. Then he'll listen to you when you say where you're right.” Ludwig had said something similar at breakfast, only shorter: “Whoever listens first wins.” And Mara, who was coming off her night shift and only wanted to grab a coffee, had added: “And offer him mint tea. Not coffee. People who work nights hate being offered coffee at eleven. Then they think you don't know what their life is like.” Lena had written all three pieces of advice on a slip of paper and put it in her apron pocket.

“Dr Vogt,” Lena began, “my grandfather told me what this is about. First of all I'd like to apologise. We never thought that someone above the café has to sleep during the day. It wasn't a lack of consideration. It was simply thoughtlessness.” Dr Vogt nodded slowly. “I believe you,” he said. “And I don't want to end up as the neighbour who spoils everyone's fun either. I've heard what this bell means here. The woman at the kiosk told me, at length, with all the details.” Lena had to smile. Mrs Becker at the kiosk told everything at length and with all the details, even things that had never happened.

“But,” Dr Vogt went on, and his voice grew firmer, “I have to point out to you that for four weeks I haven't slept more than three hours at a stretch. I've counted. Yesterday, between twelve and four, it rang sixty-three times. I'm an anaesthetist. When I operate at night, my patients sleep because I'm awake. And I can only be awake if I sleep during the day.” He paused. “I'm afraid it can't go on like this. If we don't find a solution, I'll have to go to the landlord. I wouldn't want that. But I would have to.”

Lena wrote “63” in her notebook and underlined it twice. Then she looked up. “I fully understand your annoyance,” she said, and she meant it. “I get up at four every morning, because of the bakery. If someone wakes me at two in the afternoon, I'm not friendly either. I suggest the following: what would you say if the bell wasn't used during quiet hours, that is between one and three? We'll put a cloth over it. And in the morning, before you go to bed, maybe not then either?” Dr Vogt did the maths. “I sleep from nine to four,” he said. “That would be seven hours without the bell. Almost the whole day. Then it's not a bell any more. Then it's a monument.”

Lena realised they had reached a point where they couldn't go any further. She didn't want to turn the bell into a monument. He didn't want to stay awake for seven hours. They were both right. And at that moment the door opened and Hotte came in, as he did every Thursday, with his tram driver's cap and his stick, and before anyone could stop him, he pulled the bell cord. Twice. Hard. Dr Vogt flinched as if someone had hit him. Hotte looked at him, then at Lena, then at him again. “What's goin' on here?” he asked. “Looks like a divorce.”

Lena explained, briefly, and expected Hotte to get angry, since the bell was, after all, a little bit his too. But Hotte didn't get angry. He sat down at the table without asking, took off his cap and gave Dr Vogt a long look with his small, lively eyes. “Night shift,” he said at last, and it wasn't a question. “How long?” “Eighteen years,” said Dr Vogt. Hotte nodded. “I did thirty-one years on nights. At the depot. Erna used to say she was married to a ghost. The worst wasn't the night. The worst was the day. When everyone else is livin' and you've gotta sleep.”

He told how in the seventies he used to take the last trams back to the depot at night, at half past one, at three, and how he walked home through the empty streets of Lichtenberg, when the bakers were just heating their ovens and the newspaper men were throwing the bundles down in front of the kiosks. “Them were my neighbours,” said Hotte. “Not the people in my block. Never saw them. My neighbours were the baker on the corner, who gave me a warm roll at four, and the newspaper bloke, who read me the headline. And Erna, when she was gettin' up and I was goin' to bed. Ten minutes a day we had. Ten minutes. Thirty-one years.” He fell silent. Then he said, a bit more quietly: “It was enough. But only 'cause we never wasted them ten minutes.”

Dr Vogt looked at Hotte and, for the first time that morning, his face softened. “That's exactly it,” he said quietly. “That's exactly what it is. I've been living here for a month and I don't know anyone. When I wake up, everyone's already back home. When I leave for work, everyone's asleep. And the only thing I catch of this house is a bell that rings when other people are happy. Or sad. But never me.” There was silence at the table. Lena put down her pen. Suddenly it was no longer about decibels and quiet hours. It was about something else.

The solution they finally agreed on ended up on a napkin, in Lena's handwriting, and was later hung beside the bell, under the old “Klingeln erlaubt” sign. It said: “Mon–Fri, 9–16: ring softly. With your finger, not the cord.” That same afternoon Andrei rigged up a little piece of felt around the bell's clapper, which could be lowered during the day, so that the bell only gave a soft, muffled sound, like a heart beating under a jumper. Elif, who was just coming home from school, tested it straight away. “You can still hear it,” she announced. “But only if you're listening.” Dr Vogt said he could live with that.

Lena still put on the table the cloth she had got ready for the bell, an old blue-and-white checked tea towel from Ingrid's kitchen. “For emergencies,” she said. “If it's too loud despite the felt, come down and hang it over the bell yourself. Without asking. It's your right now.” Dr Vogt took the tea towel, folded it carefully and put it in the pocket of his hospital jacket, next to the badge. He never used it. But he always carried it with him, as he told Lena much later, at the hospital too, on the night shift, like a piece of a house where someone had thought of him.

But that wasn't the whole solution. The other part wasn't on the napkin. It was agreed between Hotte and Dr Vogt with a handshake while Lena was in the kitchen. The following Sunday at four in the afternoon, when Dr Vogt woke up, someone knocked on his door. Outside stood Hotte, with two slices of cheesecake on a plate. “Breakfast,” he said. “For night workers it's breakfast time now. I know.” And the Sunday after that Ludwig stood at the door, with a copy of his book, and the Sunday after that Mara, who worked at the same hospital, as it turned out, just on a different ward, and who invited him for a coffee at four, her breakfast time when she was on nights.

In December, on a Monday a little after nine in the morning, when the bell was already wearing its felt, Dr Vogt came into the café after a long night. He looked even more tired than usual. Lena, who was standing behind the counter, knew without asking that something had happened. That night there had been a difficult operation, a child, an accident on Schönhauser Allee, seven hours, and the child was alive. Dr Vogt said nothing about it. He just went over to the bell, lifted the felt, very carefully, and rang. Once. Very softly, with his finger, not the cord. Then he let the felt back down, sat at the window table and ordered, for the first time, a coffee.

Lena brought it to his table herself, together with a warm roll nobody had ordered. She didn't ask what had happened in the night. She had learned from Hotte that there are some things you don't ask about. You just ring. And whoever listens hears it, even through felt. That morning, Lena would say later, the whole café heard it, even though it had been almost no sound at all.

Reading text: a letter of complaint
Read the letter that Dr Vogt almost sent to the landlord. Listen twice. At the end there are 4 questions.
Dear Mr Kühn, I have been living on the first floor of Kastanienallee 33 since 1 October.
I'm afraid I have to complain about a regular disturbance of the peace: in the café on the ground floor a loud bell is rung up to sixty times a day, including during quiet hours.
As I work as a doctor on the night shift, I am unable to sleep during the day because of this.
I would therefore ask you to find a solution with the owner of the café. I would be glad to hear from you by the end of the month. Yours sincerely, Dr Konrad Vogt
Handwritten note: Not sent. Problem solved. With cheesecake.
